issues.legal_issue: A shared household is not limited to a home owned or rented by the husband or to joint-family property in which he has a share, but must be a dwelling in which the aggrieved person lived in a domestic relationship with some degree of permanence.
material_facts: The daughter-in-law had lived in the father-in-law’s house since her marriage and continued to occupy part of it.
The father-in-law claimed exclusive ownership, and the husband was said to have no share in the property.
The daughter-in-law claimed a right of residence and alleged domestic violence in proceedings under the domestic-violence legislation.
issues.conclusion: A shared household need not be owned or rented by the husband or belong to a joint family of which he is a member. The contrary interpretation in S.R. Batra v. Taruna Batra was incorrect. The phrase covering a household where the aggrieved person has lived does not make every place of fleeting or casual residence a shared household; the character and permanence of the living arrangement and the parties’ intention must be considered.
issues.legal_principle: The exhaustive definition in Section 2(s), read with Sections 17 and 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, does not require the aggrieved person or her husband to hold an ownership interest. Its requirement is a household where the aggrieved person lives or has lived in a domestic relationship, subject to the nature and permanence of the residence. The Court relied on the interpretive approach to “means” and “includes” in Bharat Coop. Bank (Mumbai) Ltd. v. Coop. Bank Employees Union and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India, and on the purpose of the Act discussed in Kunapareddy Alias Nookala Shanka Balaji v. Kunapareddy Swarna Kumari and Manmohan Attavar v. Neelam Manmohan Attavar. It held that S.R. Batra v. Taruna Batra did not correctly interpret Section 2(s).

predicates.domestic_violence_residence_case: The proceeding concerns a person seeking a right of residence on the basis of domestic violence within a domestic relationship.
predicates.aggrieved_person_lived_in_domestic_relat: The person seeking residence lived in the household in a domestic relationship with the respondent, either alone or with the respondent.
predicates.residence_was_not_merely_casual: The person’s living arrangement had some permanence, assessed in light of the parties’ intention and the nature of the household.

issues.definition: When a residence claim arising from domestic violence rests on a non-casual period of living in a domestic relationship, the home may be shared even if the husband has no property interest in it.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not enter judgment on admission in a property suit when the defendant raises a substantial, unresolved defence to dispossession and the asserted admission is not clear, unambiguous, and unconditional.
material_facts: The owner sought mandatory and permanent injunctions to remove his daughter-in-law from part of the house.

The daughter-in-law admitted in separate domestic-violence pleadings that the property stood in the father-in-law’s name, but in her written statement disputed that it was his self-acquired property and asserted that it had been acquired with joint-family funds.
She also asserted a right to reside in the property as a shared household.
The Trial Court decreed the suit under Order XII Rule 6 based on the ownership admission without deciding those defences.
issues.conclusion: The Trial Court’s decree under Order XII Rule 6 was unsustainable; the substantial defences and the claim of residence had to be considered rather than disposed of summarily on the alleged admission.
issues.legal_principle: Order XII Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure is discretionary, not a matter of right. Under Himani Alloys Ltd. v. Tata Steel Ltd., an admission relied on for judgment without trial must be clear, unambiguous, unconditional, categorical, and deliberate. S.M. Asif v. Virender Kumar Bajaj holds that judgment on admission is inappropriate where the defence raises objections going to the root of the case. Section 26 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 also permits relevant residence relief to be sought in other legal proceedings.

predicates.civil_property_injunction_case: An owner has brought a civil suit seeking an injunction or possession affecting the defendant’s occupancy of property.
predicates.defendant_disputes_material_property_or_: The defendant contests a material issue about the property or asserts a legal right to remain in the home.
predicates.alleged_admission_does_not_resolve_defen: The statement relied on as an admission does not clearly, unambiguously, and unconditionally dispose of the defendant’s material defence.

issues.definition: A court cannot summarily grant an owner’s requested injunction on an alleged admission when a civil property suit includes a material defence that the admission does not resolve.

issues.legal_issue: An aggrieved person may seek residence relief in an existing civil proceeding, and the civil court must consider a pleaded claim that the property is a shared household rather than leave it undecided merely because a separate domestic-violence proceeding is pending.
material_facts: The owner brought a civil suit seeking removal of the daughter-in-law from the house.
In her written statement, she asserted that the house was a shared household and that she had a right to reside there.
A separate application under the domestic-violence legislation was also pending.
issues.conclusion: The residence claim could be considered in the civil suit under Section 26, and the Trial Court’s failure to consider it defeated a right protected by the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 26 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 permits relief available under Sections 18 to 22, including residence relief under Section 19, to be sought in a legal proceeding before a civil, family, or criminal court, in addition to other relief. In Vaishali Abhimanyu Joshi v. Nanasaheb Gopal Joshi, the Court held that Section 26 must be interpreted to effectuate the Act’s purpose and that considering the claim in the existing proceeding avoids multiplicity of proceedings.

predicates.civil_proceeding_affects_aggrieved_perso: A civil court proceeding concerns the aggrieved person’s occupancy or other rights in the property.
predicates.defendant_pleads_shared_household_reside: The defendant asserts in the civil proceeding that the home is a shared household and that she is entitled to reside there.

issues.definition: When a person pleads a shared-household right of residence in a civil proceeding affecting her, the civil court must consider that claim in that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A property owner may be treated as a respondent for deciding a pleaded residence claim in a civil suit, but residence relief requires the claimant to plead and prove the statutory conditions, including domestic violence by the person against whom relief is sought.
material_facts: The daughter-in-law had lived in the property with her husband and had named the father-in-law as a respondent in her application under Section 12.
In the civil suit, she relied on her asserted right of residence to resist the owner’s claim.
The Magistrate’s order was interim and rested on a prima facie assessment; the civil court had to decide the residence claim on the material before it.
issues.conclusion: For deciding the daughter-in-law’s claim under Sections 17 and 19 read with Section 26 in the suit, the owner could be treated as a respondent. But the claimant had to plead and prove the necessary conditions for relief, including that the person treated as respondent had committed an act of domestic violence.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(a) and 2(q) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005, read with the striking down of the words “adult male” in Section 2(q) by Hiral P. Harsora v. Kusum Narottamdas Harsora, allow a respondent to be a person in a domestic relationship against whom relief is sought. Sections 17, 19, and 26 permit residence relief to be considered in a civil proceeding, but relief depends on proof of the statutory requirements, including domestic violence. A prima facie interim order in the separate proceeding does not itself establish those requirements for the civil court’s decision.

predicates.civil_suit_involves_domestic_violence_re: The civil suit requires determination of a claimed right of residence arising under domestic-violence law.
predicates.property_owner_was_in_domestic_relations: The property owner lived with the claimant in a household in a relationship falling within the statutory definition of domestic relationship.
predicates.claimant_seeks_relief_against_owner: The claimant seeks relief against the property owner, either in the domestic-violence proceeding or by relying on the claimed right in the civil suit.
predicates.claimant_proves_domestic_violence_by_own: The claimant establishes in the proceeding that the property owner committed an act of domestic violence against her.

issues.definition: A property owner in a domestic relationship may be treated as a respondent for a residence claim, but relief against that owner depends on the claimant proving domestic violence and the other statutory conditions.

issues.legal_issue: The right to reside in a shared household does not prevent a competent court from deciding a properly instituted suit for eviction or exclusion, because dispossession may occur in accordance with the procedure established by law.
material_facts: The Magistrate’s interim order restrained dispossession without an order of a competent court.
The owner subsequently brought a civil suit seeking mandatory and permanent injunctions against the daughter-in-law.
The daughter-in-law asserted that the property was a shared household and that she had a right to reside there.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit was maintainable, and a competent court could decide whether eviction or exclusion was justified on the facts and evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(2) of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 expressly permits eviction or exclusion from a shared household in accordance with the procedure established by law. The Court interpreted this to include proceedings in a competent court, and held that the Act contains no bar to such civil proceedings. By analogy, it considered the meaning of “evicted therefrom in due course of law” in Section 145(6) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as explained in Shanti Kumar Panda v. Shakuntala Devi.

predicates.civil_eviction_or_exclusion_case: A civil proceeding seeks to remove or exclude a person from a home she claims as a shared household.
predicates.claimant_asserts_shared_household_right: The person facing removal asserts a right of residence in the home as a shared household.
predicates.owner_seeks_relief_through_competent_cou: The owner seeks removal through a properly instituted proceeding before a court competent to decide the parties’ rights.

issues.definition: An asserted shared-household right does not bar an owner from bringing a civil eviction proceeding in a competent court.

issues.legal_issue: A husband is not automatically a necessary party in every suit concerning his wife’s claimed residence in a shared household, though he may be a proper party when his presence would assist complete adjudication of the issues.
material_facts: The father-in-law sued his daughter-in-law without joining her husband.
The daughter-in-law relied on her statutory residence claim, and the possible availability of alternate accommodation and maintenance responsibilities could involve the husband.
The High Court directed that husbands be impleaded in all such cases.
issues.conclusion: The husband was not a necessary party in the suit, but could be a proper party. The High Court’s general direction for impleadment in all cases was too broad; the trial court must exercise its discretion under Order I Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the circumstances of each case.
issues.legal_principle: Order I Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers a court to add a party whose presence is necessary to enable effective and complete adjudication. The Court applied the principles in Razia Begum v. Sahebzadi Anwar Begum and Ramesh Hirachand Kundanmal v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay, distinguishing a necessary party from a proper party.

predicates.civil_shared_household_suit: A civil suit concerns an owner’s claim to remove a person who asserts a right of residence in a shared household.
predicates.husband_is_not_claimed_against: The plaintiff has not sought relief against the husband.
predicates.husbands_role_may_assist_complete_adjudi: The husband’s potential responsibility for maintenance or alternate accommodation may assist the court in resolving the residence claim.

issues.definition: In a civil shared-household suit, the husband need not be joined merely because of the relationship, but may be joined when his presence would help resolve the issues.

issues.legal_issue: Pending domestic-violence proceedings and orders granting interim or final residence relief do not bar related civil proceedings; those orders are relevant evidence, but the civil court must decide the civil issues on the evidence before it and is not bound by the domestic-violence court’s findings.
material_facts: The daughter-in-law’s application under the domestic-violence legislation was pending when the owner filed the civil suit.
The Magistrate had made an interim order against dispossession without an order of a competent court.
The civil suit concerned the same property and the claimed right of residence.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit could be initiated and continued. Any interim or final order under Section 19 was relevant and had to be given due weight as evidence, but it did not bind the civil court or prevent it from deciding the issues independently on the evidence led there.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17, 19, 25, 26, 28, and 36 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 contemplate independent proceedings and do not bar civil proceedings; Section 43 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes the domestic-violence order relevant in the circumstances described. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras, K.G. Premshankar v. Inspector of Police, Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, Seth Ramdayal Jat v. Laxmi Prasad, and the principles concerning the limited evidentiary effect of criminal-court orders discussed in Shanti Kumar Panda v. Shakuntala Devi. The two proceedings must be decided on the evidence before their respective courts; a domestic-violence order is not conclusive in the civil suit.

predicates.civil_proceeding_and_domestic_violence_p: A civil proceeding and a domestic-violence proceeding concern the same home or claimed right of residence.
predicates.domestic_violence_court_has_made_residen: The court in the domestic-violence proceeding has made an interim or final order concerning residence.

issues.definition: A residence order in a related domestic-violence proceeding may be considered as evidence, but it neither stops the civil case nor determines its outcome.

issues.legal_issue: A claimed right of residence in a shared household is not indefeasible, and a court deciding residence relief must balance the claimant’s interests with the interests of other occupants, including elderly owners.
material_facts: The claimant was the daughter-in-law of the owner and occupied part of the home while marital discord existed between her and her husband.
The owner was an elderly person who asserted a need to live peacefully in his own home.
The High Court directed that the competing residence interests and the possibility of alternate accommodation be considered on remand.
issues.conclusion: The right to reside is not indefeasible. Courts must balance the rights of both sides when granting relief, and the High Court’s directions were considered to adequately balance those rights.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 19 of the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 confer a right of residence and authorize residence orders, including provision for alternate accommodation or rent under Section 19(1)(f). The Court held that relief under the Act or in civil proceedings must balance the rights of the aggrieved person and the other occupants, particularly where an elderly father-in-law or mother-in-law is affected.

predicates.domestic_violence_residence_case: The court is deciding a claim for residence relief arising from domestic violence.
predicates.claimant_seeks_to_remain_in_shared_house: The claimant seeks to continue living in a home asserted to be a shared household.
predicates.other_occupant_has_competing_residence_i: Another occupant, including an elderly owner, has a competing interest in living in or using the home.

issues.definition: When a residence claimant and another occupant have competing interests in a shared household, the court must balance those interests and may account for alternate accommodation when shaping relief.
